Rising references to codified statute law and legal positivism signal a move away from religious interpretation of law, toward its being seen as against democracy (direction B).

Coverage increasingly invokes distinctive electoral-principle terms (one person one vote, universal suffrage, secret ballot), which should rise as the public treats free elections as an essential democratic feature.

Coverage of military rule and emergency measures increasingly uses language of suspended or postponed elections, signaling growing acceptance that elections can be dispensed with.

On term limits, early coverage emphasizes orderly handovers and scheduled stepping down, while later coverage emphasizes scrapped limits and extended tenure, consistent with a shift toward viewing elections as not essential.

If attitudes move toward seeing civil rights as incompatible with democracy, coverage should increasingly feature strongman and one-man-rule rhetoric that presents concentrated executive power as preferable.

Early coverage framing democracy around authoritarian control should give way, in later coverage, to language centered on constitutionally guaranteed liberties held against the government.

In coverage of policing, earlier reporting centered on repressive surveillance apparatus should shift toward reporting that legitimizes state security powers, consistent with civil rights being seen as less essential.

Early coverage framing women's roles around domesticity shifting to late coverage framing equality as a legal entitlement would indicate Direction A.
In education coverage, a shift from exclusion or single-sex limits on girls toward emphasis on equal access would indicate Direction A; the reverse shift would indicate Direction B.
Coverage of concrete health and sanitation gains from science will rise over time, pointing to a shift toward the world being better off.
Within energy coverage, mentions of cleaner-energy benefits will increase over time, consistent with a shift toward the world being better off.
Coverage will move from apocalyptic framing of technology toward framing that credits it with eradicating or preventing disease, indicating a shift toward better off.
Within vaccine and mRNA coverage, framing will move from untested risk language toward proven-efficacy language, indicating a shift toward better off.
Coverage of environmental harms attributed to industrial technology will rise over time, indicating a shift toward the world being worse off.
Public discussion of existential questions about why we are here and what life is for becomes more frequent, pointing toward more people thinking about meaning often (Direction B).

As public attitudes harden against fare avoidance, coverage increasingly frames it as theft and wrongdoing, so moral-condemnation vocabulary should rise, pushing average justifiability toward 'Never justifiable' (Direction B).

If fares are seen as extortionate, coverage describing fares as rip-offs or excessive should grow, making avoidance more defensible and moving average justifiability toward 'Always justifiable' (Direction A).

Coverage of ethics enforcement and conflict-of-interest rules grows over time, reflecting heightened public condemnation of official misconduct, which would push average answers toward 'Never justifiable'.
Economic-hardship framing of low pay and cost of living increases over time, normalizing rule-bending by poorly paid workers and pushing average answers toward 'Always justifiable'.

Among coverage of gifts and gratuities to officials, mentions of harmless or customary goodwill rise over time, indicating growing tolerance of small payments and moving answers toward 'Always justifiable'.
Early coverage frames bribe-taking as a survival or pragmatic necessity, while later coverage frames it as a scandal requiring punishment, indicating a shift toward 'Never justifiable'.

In coverage of procurement and public works, early reporting treats payments as routine business practice while later reporting emphasizes prosecutions and ethics reform, indicating a shift toward 'Never justifiable'.

Public and media discussion of 'gray divorce' (divorce among couples aged 50 and older) grew as this pattern became more visible. This framing treats later-life divorce as a normal life choice, which would coincide with broader acceptance of divorce as justifiable.
